# R8 Digest — Epilogue (2 Sam 21–24) — Tsumura NICOT

**Source slice:** `R8_epilogue_21-24_11169-13317.txt`  
**Raw lines:** 11169–13317  
**Scope:** VI. Epilogue (21:1–24:25) — famine/Gibeonites; Philistine wars; Song of David (22≈Ps 18); Last Words (23:1–7); heroes; census/plague/Araunah  
**Attribution:** claims are Tsumura’s unless marked as his report of another scholar’s view

### C-R8-01
**Claim:** Those who treat 2 Samuel mainly as a Succession Narrative regard chs. 21–24 as an appendix and hold that the main narrative flows from 2 Sam. 20 to 1 K. 1; Tsumura rejects this and holds that the four chapters are a tightly organized literary unit forming the epilogue of the entire book (1–2 Samuel), corresponding to the prologue (1 Sam. 1–7).  
**Quote:** “Those who take 2 Samuel basically as a Succession Narrative (SN) treat the last four chapters, chs. 21-24, as an appendix and hold that the main narrative flows from 2 Sam. 20 to 1 K. 1. However, these four chapters themselves are a tightly organized literary unit and form the epilogue of the entire book, i.e., 1–2 Samuel, corresponding to the prologue (1 Sam. 1-7).”  
**Locus:** R8 slice ll. 5–7; Epilogue intro  
**Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R8-02
**Claim:** The poems of the prologue and epilogue—Song of Hannah (1 Sam. 2:1–10) and David’s Song (2 Sam. 22) and Last Words (23:1–7)—constitute an inclusio of the entire narrative; the overall structure of 1–2 Samuel strengthens and focuses the main themes of monarchy, the Davidic kingdom, and David’s royal throne.  
**Quote:** “The poems in the prologue and the epilogue, that is, the Song of Hannah (1 Sam. 2:1-10) and David’s Song (2 Sam. 22) and Last Words (23:1-7), constitute an inclusio of the entire narrative. Thus the overall structure of 1–2 Samuel as a whole strengthens and focuses on the main themes of the entire book, that is, the monarchy, the Davidic kingdom and the royal throne of David.”  
**Locus:** R8 ll. 7–8  
**Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[david-tsumura]], [[davidic-covenant]], [[david]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R8-03
**Claim:** Tsumura’s outline of 1–2 Samuel places VI. Epilogue (2 Sam. 21:1–24:25) after V. “Story of King David” (2 Sam. 1:1–20:26), with the Epilogue subdivided ABXX′B′A′: A famine/Saul’s sons (21:1–14); B Philistine war (21:15–22); X Song of David (22:1–51 = Ps. 18); X′ Last Words (23:1–7); B′ David’s heroes (23:8–39); A′ census and the Lord’s anger (24:1–25).  
**Quote:** “VI.Epilogue (2 Sam. 21:1–24:25) / A.Famine and the Death of Saul’s Sons (21:1-14) / B.Philistine War (21:15-22) / X.Song of David (22:1-51) = Ps. 18 / X′.Last Words of David (23:1-7) / B′.David’s Heroes (23:8-39) / A′.Census and the Lord’s Anger (24:1-25)”  
**Locus:** R8 ll. 22–35  
**Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R8-04
**Claim:** The AXB pattern appears in both Prologue and Epilogue; the Epilogue is a chiastic arrangement with two poems (X and X′) at the center, framed by two lists-with-narrative (B and B′), themselves framed by first and last narrative sections sharing the theme of death as the result of God’s anger.  
**Quote:** “It should be noted that the AXB pattern appears both in the Prologue and in the Epilogue. The Epilogue is a chiastic arrangement: two poems (X and X′) are in the center, framed by two lists with narrative, B and B′, which are framed by the first and last sections, which are both narratives with the theme of death as the result of God’s anger.”  
**Locus:** R8 ll. 37–37  
**Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R8-05
**Claim:** Narratives are not chronological: Song (ch. 22 = Ps. 18) is probably from earlier in David’s life (possibly before he became king), Last Words (23:1–7) from his last days; narrative sections A–B–B′–A′ seem sequential; ch. 24 is climactic, leading to purchase of the land for Solomon’s temple. Literary structure is a kind of AXB, i.e. ABXX′B′A′, with the two poems inserted into the narrative flow A-B-B′-A′.  
**Quote:** “The narratives are not placed in chronological order, however, for the first poem (ch. 22 = Ps. 18) is probably from the earlier part of David’s life, possibly even before he became king, and the second (23:1-7) from the last days of his life. On the other hand, the narrative sections (A, B, E and F) seem to be sequential. The last section (ch. 24) is climactic, describing the events leading to the purchase of the land upon which Solomon would build the temple. Thus, I analyze the literary structure here as a kind of the AXB pattern, i.e., ABXX′B′A′, where the two poems in chs. 22 (X) and 23 (X′), are inserted into the narrative flow of A-B-B′-A′.”  
**Locus:** R8 ll. 39–39  
**Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[david-tsumura]], [[david]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R8-06
**Claim (footnote revision):** In *The First Book of Samuel* Tsumura had taken 2 Sam. 21–24 as concentric ABCBA; he now revises it as a complex AXB pattern, ABXX′B′A′. Other scholars (Anderson; Dietrich) designate A-B-C-C′-B′-A′, but because C/C′ are poetic and the others narrative, Tsumura prefers AXB over simple ABA chiastic labeling.  
**Quote:** “In my The First Book of Samuel, p. 67, I took 2 Sam. 21-24 as constituting a concentric structure, the ABCBA pattern. But, I now revise it as a complex AXB pattern, i.e., ABXX′B′A′. … the C/C′ are poetic, while the others are narrative, hence it seems we have here the AXB pattern rather than the chiastic pattern ABA.”  
**Locus:** R8 ll. 1607–1613 (nn. 3–4)  
**Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R8-08
**Claim:** Famine for three years was because of Saul’s attempt to exterminate the Gibeonites, who were protected by Joshua-era oath (Josh 9:3–27); no other direct biblical mention of the incident, but it may stand behind 2 Sam. 4:2–3. Famine expresses divine wrath for Saul’s treaty violation; leaders’ failures may have to be sorted out by successors.  
**Quote:** “A famine had afflicted Israel for three years because of Saul’s attempt to exterminate the Gibeonites, who were protected by an oath sworn in the time of Joshua (Josh 9:3-27). There is no other direct mention of the incident in the Bible, but it may be in the background of 2 Sam. 4:2-3 (see commentary). The famine was an expression of divine wrath against King Saul’s violation of the treaty. This incident illustrates how serious the consequences may be when the leader of God’s people offends God’s righteousness. But we don’t know why God did not punish Saul at the time. Generally speaking, leaders’ failures must be sorted out by their successors, if the justice is to prevail.”  
**Locus:** R8 ll. 62–62; on 21:1  
**Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[saul]], [[david]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R8-09
**Claim:** Tsumura reports C. H. Gordon on ANE king–land fertility correspondence (Odyssey 19:109–14 vs. Oedipus Rex blight); and Malamat/Fensham on treaty-violation causality (Hittite plague prayers of Mursili II): national disaster may arise from past violation of a treaty oath—common Israelite and Hittite doctrine of causality.  
**Quote:** “Regarding the present incident, C. H. Gordon calls our attention to the fact that ‘the fitness (physical and moral) and deportment of kings were serious matters, for they were believed to bring on a corresponding state of land and people.’ … According to Malamat and Fensham, the incident is to be taken as a case of punishment for treaty violations in the ancient Near East. Looking at Hittite texts such as the so-called plague prayers of the fourteenth century Hittite king Mursili II, Malamat identifies ‘a common doctrine of causality’ in both Israelite and Hittite literatures according to which ‘a national disaster (famine, plague, etc.) might arise from a past violation of a treaty oath.’”  
**Locus:** R8 ll. 64–66  
**Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[saul]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R8-10
**Claim:** “Due to Saul and his bloody house” (ʾel-šāʾûl weʾel-bêt haddāmîm) is an incomplete sentence (aposiopesis), not “confused wording” (Budde); lit. “to Saul and to the house of the blood,” response to “Why did this famine occur?” “His bloody house” means bloodguilt on/of his house, not simply bloodshed of his house.  
**Quote:** “Due to Saul and his bloody house (ʾel-šāʾûl weʾel-bêt haddāmîm) is an incomplete sentence, not a ‘confused wording’ (Budde), and is literally ‘to Saul and to the house of the blood.’ It is presumably uttered in response to such a question as, ‘Why did this famine occur?’ … The Hebrew expression his bloody house means ‘bloodguilt on his house’ (see NRSV; also McCarter) or ‘the bloodguilt of his house’ (JPS), not simply ‘bloodshed of his house.’”  
**Locus:** R8 ll. 70–70  
**Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[saul]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R8-11
**Claim:** Gibeonites are remnant of the Amorites (pre-Israelite inhabitants); though Israel had sworn alliance with them, Saul sought to strike them out “in his zeal for the sons of Israel and Judah.” A king should not do such an unlawful thing against God’s will even in zeal for the covenant people; his “bloody house” bore bloodguilt for this violence.  
**Quote:** “The remnant of the Amorites refers to the pre-Israelite inhabitants of the land. Though the Israelites had sworn to, i.e., made an alliance with, the Gibeonites, Saul had conducted bloodshed against them in his zeal for his people of Israel and Judah. A king should not do such an unlawful thing against God’s will even in his zeal for the covenant people of God. In other words, his ‘bloody [from bloodshed] house’ bore ‘bloodguilt’ for this violence.”  
**Locus:** R8 ll. 116–116; on 21:2  
**Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[saul]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R8-13
**Claim:** Gibeonites request seven men from Saul’s sons to hang before the LORD in Gibeah of Saul; seven is a symbolic number. This conflicts with Deut. 24:16 (children not put to death for fathers); the text does not suggest the seven were accomplices, and chronologically even Merab’s oldest son could scarcely have been ten when Saul died. Exposure of corpse was probably part of ANE punishment for treaty violation (Fensham).  
**Quote:** “Seven men is a symbolic number of Saul’s descendants. In order that God be entreated (v. 14), these seven sons were to be hanged before the LORD. This of course was against the command ‘nor shall children be put to death because of their fathers’ (Deut. 24:16). Were these seven accomplices of Saul’s act? The text does not suggests that, and furthermore, as David must have been at least in his late teens when Merab married (1 Sam. 18:19) and was no more than thirty when Saul died (2 Sam. 5:4), even Merab’s oldest son could scarcely have been ten when Saul died. … Such exposure of the corpse was probably ‘part of the punishment for a treaty violation elsewhere in the ancient Near East.’”  
**Locus:** R8 ll. 126–128; on 21:6  
**Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[saul]], [[david]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R8-14
**Claim:** McCarter (after Wellhausen) emends “Gibeah of Saul, the chosen of the LORD” toward “(to Yahweh-)in-Gibeon on the mountain of Yahweh”; Tsumura rejects the h/ḥ scribal-error hypothesis and McCarter’s “Gibeonite Yahweh, local manifestation” theory.  
**Quote:** “For the phrase Gibeah of Saul, the chosen of the LORD (begibʿat Šāʾûl beḥîr YHWH), McCarter suggests reading it as ‘(to Yahweh-)in-Gibeon on the mountain of Yahweh,’ following Wellhausen … However, such a scribal error (i.e., h for ḥ) occurs less likely than has been asserted. Also there is no support for his hypothesis that this refers to ‘the Gibeonite Yahweh, the local manifestation of the national god’…”  
**Locus:** R8 ll. 130–130  
**Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[saul]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R8-15
**Claim:** David spares Mephibosheth son of Jonathan because of the LORD’s oath between David and Jonathan; this Mephibosheth must be distinguished from Mephibosheth son of Saul (v. 8). Tsumura rejects the view that ch. 9 originally followed this incident and that v. 7 is a secondary insertion; both here and in ch. 9 David remembered his oath (1 Sam. 20:14–16).  
**Quote:** “It is often asserted that David found out about Mephibosheth only after this incident, so originally ch. 9 was placed after this incident and this verse was inserted when the material was separated. However, this is unnecessary; see the commentary on ch. 9. Mephibosheth, son of Jonathan here should be distinguished from Mephibosheth in v. 8 who is the son of Saul; see on 4:4. Both in ch. 9 and here David remembered his oath to his friend Jonathan and his descendants (1 Sam. 20:14-16).”  
**Locus:** R8 ll. 146–146; on 21:7  
**Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[david]], [[jonathan]], [[saul]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R8-16
**Claim:** Leningrad Codex reads five sons of Michal, but Michal was childless (2 Sam. 6:23) and Adriel was Merab’s husband (1 Sam. 18:19); “Michal” is likely a scribal error substituting a more familiar name. David hands over Armoni and Mephibosheth (Rizpah) plus Merab’s five; they are hanged on the mountain before the LORD at beginning of barley harvest (April).  
**Quote:** “For the five sons of Merab the Leningrad Codex reads ‘the five sons of Michal,’ but we know that Michal was childless (see 2 Sam. 6:23) and furthermore that Adriel was the husband of her sister Merab (1 Sam. 18:19). So ‘Michal’ is likely a scribal error, substituting a more familiar name for a less familiar name.”  
**Locus:** R8 ll. 150–154; on 21:8–9  
**Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[saul]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R8-17
**Claim:** Rizpah’s vigil from harvest until rain may imply bodies were not to be buried until rains fell (famine stopped); David’s earlier burial may have prompted God’s response (v. 14), probably by rain. Horror of unburied corpses (1 Sam. 17; Deut. 21:22–23; Homer; Ahab/Jezebel).  
**Quote:** “Until rain fell on them, possibly implies that ‘the rain should have fallen upon them.’ Perhaps it had been decided that they would not be buried until the rains fell (and the famine stopped). That would suggest that when David heard what Rizpah was doing (v. 11) he buried them earlier than planned, and then God responded (v. 14), probably by rain.”  
**Locus:** R8 ll. 156–158; on 21:10  
**Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[david]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R8-18
**Claim:** David recovers bones of Saul and Jonathan from Jabesh-gilead and buries them (with the hanged) in Zela, grave of Kish; God “responded to the plea for the land” (*ʿtr). In both 21:14 and 24:25, God’s anger is finally appeased by David’s conduct—here burying bones, in ch. 24 sacrifices at the designated place. Proper burial essential for welfare of dead and living (Ugaritic KTU 1.161).  
**Quote:** “And God responded to the plea for the land after that. … God ‘was entreated’ (*ʿtr): or ‘God was pleaded with’ (HALOT, p. 905) implies that God heard and responded. The expression also appears at 24:25. In both instances, God’s anger was finally appeased by David’s conduct — here by burying the bones, and in ch. 24 by the sacrifices at the designated place.”  
**Locus:** R8 ll. 170–182; on 21:12–14  
**Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[david]], [[saul]], [[jonathan]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R8-19
**Claim:** 21:15–22 is an excerpt about four fights of David’s men with Philistine giants (descendants of “the giant” / rāpāh, popularly Rephaim / Rapiʾu). Abishai saves weary David from Ishbi-benob; men swear David shall not go out again so as not to extinguish “the lamp of Israel” (nēr Yiśrāʾēl)—David as symbolic leader of the covenant people and Yahweh’s anointed; Firth on lamp symbolism for Davidic monarchy (1 K. 11:36 etc.).  
**Quote:** “It is an account of four fights of David’s men with Philistine giants. … The expression the lamp of Israel (nēr Yiśrāʾēl) appears only here; for a similar idea about the importance of the king, see 18:3. But, here, it explains David not so much as a military leader as a symbolic figure of a leader of the covenant people Israel. David was certainly Yahweh’s anointed king and, as D. G. Firth holds, ‘the lamp symbolism (nēr) is important for the Davidic monarchy (1 K. 11:36; 15:4; 2 K. 8:19; 2 Chr. 21:7).’”  
**Locus:** R8 ll. 219–227; on 21:15–17  
**Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[david]], [[davidic-covenant]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R8-20
**Claim:** Elhanan struck down Goliath the Gittite (21:19), causing controversy with 1 Sam. 17. Suggestions range from lost “Lahmi the brother of” (1 Chr. 20:5 parallel) to attributing Elhanan’s deed to David; Tsumura tends to hold the passages refer to two different men called Goliath by the Israelites—golyāt possibly a common Philistine giant name (Goliath Inscription Alwt/Wlt at Tell eṣ-Ṣâfī).  
**Quote:** “Elhanan. . . struck down Goliath the Gittite. Since in 1 Sam. 17 David killed Goliath from Gath … this statement has caused endless controversy. Suggestions … range from saying that the phrase ‘Lahmi the brother of’ has fallen out … to saying that the deed of Elhanan was later attributed to David. Other suggestions are that the name ‘Goliath’ became attached to David’s anonymous victim or, as I tend to hold, that the passages refer to two different men called Goliath by the Israelites. … It is possible that the name and its variants became a common name used by the Israelites to refer to a Philistine giant…”  
**Locus:** R8 ll. 233–237  
**Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[david]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R8-22
**Claim:** Chs. 22 and 23 are both songs of David—first with title alluding to beginning of his reign, second to its end. Song of David is essentially the same psalm as Ps. 18; many Hebrew spelling differences: Psalms uses “standard” spelling for worship; Samuel is more phonetic/aural (poem within narrative meant to be heard). Two theories of relation (David’s standard→Samuel phonetic; or original phonetic court collection→Psalms modernized).  
**Quote:** “Chapters 22 and 23 both are songs of David, the first with a title alluding to the beginning of his reign, and the second alluding to its end. The ‘Song of David’ in ch. 22 is essentially the same psalm as Ps. 18. However, in the Hebrew text of the two passages there are many differences in spelling, etc., though few of them come across in translation. Most of these differences can be understood when one realizes that the Book of Psalms, which was regularly used in worship throughout history, uses ‘standard’ Hebrew spelling, while the spelling in the Samuel passage tends to avoid using consonant letters for long vowels and is much more phonetic in character … due to the fact that as a poem included within a narrative, it was written as it was meant to be heard, that is, aurally.”  
**Locus:** R8 ll. 253–273  
**Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[david]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R8-23
**Claim:** Non-spelling differences may reflect Samuel as David first wrote it vs. Psalm changes for choir; e.g. 2 Sam. 22 opens with vocatives culminating in “you save me,” while Ps. 18 adds “I love you, O Lord, my strength” and deletes “you save me from violence” so nouns are clearly attributive from the start.  
**Quote:** “As for the nonspelling differences, perhaps the Samuel version is as David first wrote it, but the Psalm version reflects changes that were made for various reasons either by David himself or by the choirmasters. For example, 2 Sam. 22 starts off with a series of nouns, ‘Lord, my rock and my fortress.’ … Perhaps for this reason in Ps. 18 the song was changed by adding ‘I love you, O Lord, my strength’ at the start and deleting ‘you save me from violence,’ so the nouns are clearly attributive from the beginning…”  
**Locus:** R8 ll. 277–277  
**Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[david]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R8-24
**Claim:** Similarities of the Song (esp. vv. 8–20) to Canaanite/Baal storm mythology have been overemphasized; Tsumura holds the song describes the Lord’s control over universe and nature using ANE imagery and metaphor, not simplistic adaptation from Baal myths.  
**Quote:** “The song is often said to have many similarities to Canaanite mythology, and it has even been asserted that the language, especially that of vv. 8-20, was adapted from the myths of the storm god Baal. However, that view is too simplistic, and the similarities have been overemphasized. The song rather describes the Lord’s control over the universe and the forces of nature, using a rich selection of imagery and metaphor from the ancient Near Eastern literature…”  
**Locus:** R8 ll. 279–279  
**Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[david]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R8-25
**Claim:** Heading: David spoke this song when the LORD delivered him from all his enemies, especially Saul; “in the day” does not mean one particular incident. First part (vv. 2–31) describes the fight in terms of the Lord’s actions; next (vv. 33–49) what David did thanks to the Lord who equipped him (v. 40). ANE literary tradition of titled royal hymns (Egyptian Osiris/Aten; Ugaritic Nikkal hymn with Ammurapi).  
**Quote:** “This is the heading of the song. It is essentially the same as that of Ps. 18. … The term when is literally ‘in the day.’ This does not refer to one particular incident in David’s life, though, since the text is concerned with deliverance from ‘all his enemies.’ … This song deals with battle. Its first part (vv. 2-31) describes the fight in terms of the actions of the Lord; the next section (vv. 33-49) deals with the fight against enemies in terms of what David did, thanks to the Lord who equipped him for battle (v. 40).”  
**Locus:** R8 ll. 286–297  
**Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[david]], [[saul]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R8-26
**Claim:** Opening: nine vocative titles of Yahweh; “my rock” / fortress / deliverer / shield / horn of salvation / stronghold / refuge; “you save me from violence” (absent in Ps. 18) fits the vocatives. mehullāl … YHWH with ʾeqrāʾ interrupting is AXB; yqtl in v. 4 is present conviction while vv. 5–7 qtl shift marks past experience.  
**Quote:** “O LORD … is followed by nine titles or epithets of Yahweh in the vocative. These vocatives are in keeping with the second-person verb you save me (v. 3). … The word mehullāl, translated here as the one who is worthy to be praised, and YHWH are appositional; the verb ʾeqrāʾ (‘I call upon’) interrupts the adjacency of two nominal phrases, thus constituting the AXB pattern… Since … vv. 5-7 with the change of verbal forms from yqtls to qtls as referring to David’s past experience, the yqtls in v. 4 should be taken as his present conviction.”  
**Locus:** R8 ll. 318–330; on 22:2b–4  
**Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[david]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R8-27
**Claim:** Vv. 5–6: death/destruction//Sheol/death chiastic word pairs—all four lines say “I was facing death.” Sheol here synonym for death; only twice in 1–2 Samuel (here and 1 Sam. 2:6), both poetic. “Heard” implies attentive listening and positive response—turning point; temple = God’s heavenly temple from which he comes down (v. 10).  
**Quote:** “In vv. 5-6, the two sets of word pairs constitute a chiastic order AB//BA: death - destruction // Sheol - death. All four lines say in prose, ‘I was facing death.’ … As is usual, heard does not simply mean a passive ‘hearing’; it implies an attentive listening and, usually, a positive response. This is the point at which the situation changes. Temple probably refers to God’s heavenly temple, from which he comes down in v. 10…”  
**Locus:** R8 ll. 372–376  
**Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[david]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R8-28
**Claim:** Vv. 8–16: theophany best taken as storm images (not volcano; earthquakes alone don’t cause clouds); Lord as mighty warrior on cherub/wind chariot. Compare Ugaritic Baal “Rider of the clouds,” but Lord fights David’s enemies. Vertical grammar in v. 15 (arrows//lightning). Reject Chaoskampf reading of “mighty waters” (v. 17): metaphor for distress, not creation battle.  
**Quote:** “I believe it is best to take these as storm images; describing battle in terms of storm is common both in the Bible and other Near Eastern literature. In this song, the Lord is depicted as a mighty warrior riding in a chariot drawn by the wind or a cherub. … Mighty waters (mayim rabbîm) goes back to the imagery of v. 5. The expression is sometimes taken as referring to a Chaoskampf … However, the Bible does not suggest there was any battle in connection with creation. Here, 1–2 Samuel end with God’s merciful intervention to guide David and his people to the place of worship to be reconciled with God. It is the faithfulness of the Lord that led and fulfilled the whole plan of salvation through the human agencies used by his divine purpose. This plan and purpose were finally fulfilled in the life and death of his son Jesus Christ, the Messiah (see Matt. 1:1).”
